; GENERATED by tools/guide_check.py --write from Anvil/Core/help.pbi and each
; board's help tail. Do not edit: change the help text and regenerate.
@CHAPTER Every command

@INTRO This is the monitor's own `help`, as each board prints it, so it can never say less than the board does.

Every command the monitor accepts is listed here with the text its
`help` prints. The chapters before this one explain the commands
people use most and show what they print; this chapter is the
complete list. It is generated from the help text itself by
`tools/guide_check.py --write`, and the same tool fails a commit that
changes the help without regenerating it. Lines in angle brackets are
worked out by the board when it prints them, and a line saying
"only on a board with" marks text a board prints only when it has
that capability.

@SECTION Every board

@FRAG
Every command is a whole word. The old single letters all still work
and are shown in brackets after each one, because the host tools type
them and because U-Boot's own loads and go land here too.
Every command prints something, on every path, whether it worked or
not. If one ever returns to the prompt in silence, that is a fault.

GETTING CODE IN
  receive <address> <length> <checksum>  [b]
                  the fast way in. All three numbers are hexadecimal.
                  The monitor answers rdy, the host sends that many
                  raw bytes in chunks of 1024, and one + comes back
                  per chunk. The last line is ok or crc. The checksum
                  is the IEEE reflected CRC32, polynomial EDB88320.
  srecord                               [l, loads]
                  the slow way in, and the proven one. S3 records
                  carry the data and an S7 record ends the stream. A
                  record that never arrives cannot be detected, since
                  each checksum covers only its own record, so this
                  is the one to fall back to rather than the one to
                  reach for. One bad record blocks run until an image
                  loads cleanly.
  load <name> [address]                 [f, fatload]
                  read a file off the boot medium into memory. What
                  that medium IS depends on the board - type f on
                  its own and it says, partition by partition. A path
                  may start N: for partition N - 2:/folder/file - and
                  with no N: it is partition 1. A path may instead
                  start data: - data:/models/MODEL.PMW - which means
                  under the data.path setting: one partition, leave it
                  unset (partition 1's root); two partitions,
                  settings set data.path 2:/ and settings save.
                  Quote a path with spaces; case does not matter.
                  Without an
                  address it loads at <address>. The range is checked
                  against the payload windows, and the length is the
                  file's, not yours - which is why an address that
                  looks fine can still be refused.
  mount                                 [f]
                  bring the boot medium up and report what it is,
                  loading nothing. This is the command to type when
                  load has failed, because it names the step that
                  went wrong.
  fatls [path]                          [ls]
                  list a directory: each entry's name and its size in
                  bytes, a <DIR> marker for a subdirectory, and a
                  summary line. With no path it lists the root of
                  partition 1; ls 2:/ lists partition 2, and
                  ls 2:/folder a folder on it. FAT32 and exFAT
                  partitions list any folder by long name.
                  Any keystroke stops a long listing, which then says so.
  save <name> <address> [length]
                  write that many bytes out of memory onto the boot
                  medium, replacing that file and resizing it to
                  match. The length is hexadecimal; leave it out and
                  the file keeps the size it already has. A file that
                  is not on the medium yet is created, but only when a
                  length is given, because a file that does not exist
                  has no size of its own to keep. The path takes N:
                  like load; its folder must already exist. Writing
                  is available when this board reports a writable
                  boot medium. This is how Anvil replaces files on
                  its boot filesystem, including a staged image.
  mkdir <path>
                  make a directory. Its parent must already exist.
  rm <path>                             [del]
                  remove one file, or one EMPTY directory. Nothing is
                  ever removed recursively.
  rmdir <path>
                  remove one EMPTY directory, and refuse a file.
  rename <old path> <new path>          [mv]
                  rename or move an entry within one partition. The
                  new name must not exist yet, except as the same
                  entry in a different case.

RUNNING IT
  run [address]                         [g, go]
                  jump to a payload and start it. Without an address
                  it uses the entry point of the last thing loaded,
                  or <address> if nothing has been loaded. If the
                  payload ever comes back, its x0 register is
                  printed. A stock image never comes back.
  booti [addr [initrd [fdt]]]
                  boot an arm64 Linux Image. Checks the Image magic,
                  keeps the firmware's device tree (or the fdt you give,
                  after a dash for the skipped initrd: booti addr - fdt),
                  sets x0 to it, drops from EL2 to EL1 and branches. It
                  refuses loudly rather than jump into anything that is
                  not a kernel. Does not return.
  bootm [addr [initrd [fdt]]]
                  boot a container. A legacy uImage holding a single
                  uncompressed arm64 Linux kernel is booted; a FIT
                  (.itb) is refused (no device-tree parser here); a bare
                  Image is sent to booti. Anything else is refused by name.
  boot <name>
                  THE BOOTLOADER. Read a payload container off the
                  boot medium, place its image at the address the
                  payload was BUILT for, check its SHA-256, and only
                  then enter it. No address is typed anywhere: the
                  container carries the load address, the entry
                  point, the zero-init extent and the hash, because
                  the compiler knew all four and writing them down
                  beats retyping them. The container is the .pmf file
                  the compiler writes beside the flat image.
                  It REFUSES, loudly and having done nothing, on a
                  bad magic, a version it cannot read, a length that
                  disagrees with the file, a load or zero-init range
                  that runs over the monitor or outside the payload
                  windows, an entry outside its own image, and above
                  all on a hash that does not match. The hash check
                  is mandatory and it is the last thing before the
                  jump.
  boot mem <address> [shot]
                  the same, for a container already in memory - one
                  that arrived over receive or over the air, with no
                  medium involved at any point. The word shot keeps
                  the frame the payload leaves on the screen, before
                  this monitor repaints over it; read it back with
                  the shot command.
  boot status
                  what this board would do at its next start, and
                  the four settings behind it. Bare boot is this.
  boot ok
                  clear the failure counter: the payload came up.
                  Say it when the payload is actually working -
                  saying it every boot regardless turns the
                  reboot-loop guard off.
  boot clear
                  stop booting a file at start-up. The prompt only.
  autoboot [address]                    [a]
                  the QUICK path, and a different thing from boot.
                  It takes a bare ADDRESS in DRAM, checks nothing
                  about what is there, and lives in a memory cell
                  that survives a reset but NOT a power cycle.
                  autoboot <address> arms it, autoboot 0 clears it,
                  and autoboot on its own says what it is set to. An
                  armed monitor waits about two seconds for a key
                  when it starts and then runs what it points at.
                  It is taken BEFORE boot.file, because somebody
                  typed it in this power cycle and boot.file is
                  standing configuration.
  deadman [seconds | off]               [d]
                  a watchdog that covers the NEXT payload and
                  nothing else. If the payload hangs, the board
                  resets itself instead of sitting there. It is
                  never running while you are at this prompt. The
                  seconds are decimal. The counter behind it is 20
                  bits at 65536 ticks a second, so a fraction under
                  16 seconds is the ceiling; anything larger is cut
                  down to 15 rather than 16, because a deadman that
                  fires sooner than it promised is a trap.
  last run
                  what happened to the last payload entered: it
                  returned and what x0 held, it stopped at a
                  processor exception, or the board restarted under
                  it with the deadman armed. Kept where a reset
                  cannot erase it; the first line is for tools.

LOOKING AROUND
  map
                  the whole memory map, as this image measures it:
                  what this monitor occupies and the byte count that
                  came from, every region it refuses writes to, its
                  stack top, the address to stage a file at, and both
                  payload windows. NOTHING IN IT IS A CONSTANT. This
                  program may be any size, so its extent is the size
                  of the image the firmware loaded and the low window
                  begins above it - both move when this program does.
                  The upload tools ask for this rather than assuming.
  memory <address> <count>              [m, dump, md]
                  print a block of memory as hexadecimal, up to 4096
                  bytes at a time, with 64 as the default. Both
                  numbers are hex and the count is in bytes. The
                  address is not WINDOW-checked - reading is the whole
                  point of a debugger, and being able to point it at
                  a device register block is most of its value - but
                  the BOARD is asked about it first. See force below.
                  md.b, md.w and md.l issue true 8, 16 or 32-bit reads
                  and group each line in little-endian values. The count
                  is still bytes whichever you pick. .w/.l require a
                  2-/4-byte-aligned start and a byte count containing
                  whole units; invalid ranges read nothing. A bare md
                  reads bytes, as it always did.
                  It ends by printing the byte total it dumped and the
                  grouping it used, like the rest of this family.
  readback <address> <length>
                  the same bytes, for a MACHINE instead of a person.
                  Both hex, no length limit and no default. It prints
                  a header line, the range as base64 at 48 bytes a
                  line, then the byte count and a crc32 over it:
                    readback 57400000 1812000 bytes base64
                    <64 base64 characters>  ... and 37,750 more ...
                    readback end 1812000 bytes crc32 A1B2C3D4
                  A host reads until that last line rather than waiting
                  for silence, and checks both numbers - the crc32 uses
                  the same polynomial as crc32 and as the host tools, so
                  the two answers are independent. THE PAYLOAD GOES TO
                  WHOEVER TYPED IT and to nobody else: over the network
                  console it goes to that peer at the link's own speed,
                  never through the serial port, which is what makes it
                  hundreds of times faster than reading a hex dump back.
                  The other consoles still see this command and its last
                  line - the parts a person can read. Ctrl-C stops it and
                  the closing line then says stopped, with the count and
                  checksum of what really went. base is not added.
  write <address> <value>               [w, poke]
                  write one 32-bit word and read it straight back.
                  Both hex. The address must be a multiple of four,
                  and an address inside the monitor is refused.
  compare <first> <second> <count>      [cmp]
                  compare two blocks and name the first byte that
                  differs, and its address on both sides. Hex. A bare
                  compare counts BYTES (U-Boot's cmp counts words);
                  compare.b/.w/.l count bytes, halfwords or words.
  copy <source> <destination> <count>   [cp]
                  copy a block. Hex, overlapping ranges are safe, and
                  the destination's caches are flushed so it can be
                  run. A bare copy counts BYTES; copy.b/.w/.l count
                  bytes, halfwords or words.
  crc32 <address> <count>               [checksum]
                  the CRC32 of a block. No size limit - a whole boot
                  image is the point of it. This is how you check an
                  image before or after save writes it: tools/anvil.py
                  computes the same value on the host from the same
                  polynomial, so the two agree independently or they
                  do not. Any keystroke stops it and a stopped one
                  prints no checksum at all.
  sha1sum <address> <count>
  sha256sum <address> <count>
                  a cryptographic checksum of a block, lowercase hex, the
                  same as the sha1sum / sha256sum tools on any machine -
                  so a published image's checksum can be checked against
                  what is actually in memory. Like crc32: no size limit,
                  and a stopped one prints no digest.
  crypto [vectors | speed [kb] | list | <module>]
                  the known-answer self-test for every crypto module,
                  run HERE, on the same vectors the desktop gates use -
                  RFC 3174, 2202, 4231, 5869, 6070, 3394, FIPS-197, the
                  NIST CAVP files and the NIST/McGrew GCM table. One line
                  per vector with its CNTPCT_EL0 ticks; every GCM vector
                  is decrypted again with one bit of its tag flipped and
                  the forgery must be REFUSED. crypto speed adds one
                  throughput line per module - all eleven, over a 64 KB
                  buffer - which is the one number a desktop model cannot
                  produce. Two of the eleven cannot be given 64 KB and each
                  says under its own rate what it ran and what capped it.
                  Not one vector is typed into the image; they are
                  generated from the documents. Any keystroke stops it,
                  and a stopped sweep prints no verdict.
  fill <address> <value> [count]        [mw]
                  set a range to one value. A bare fill writes 32-bit
                  WORDS and count defaults to 1, which is what U-Boot's
                  mw does; fill.b/.w/.l write and count bytes, halfwords
                  or words. The byte count is always printed.
  mm <address>                          modify memory, interactive
  nm <address>                          the same, address held
                  a sub-prompt shows one address and its value at a
                  time. Type a hex value to write it, Enter to keep it,
                  . or q or Ctrl-C to quit - the way out is on every
                  line. mm steps to the next location, nm stays put.
                  mm.b/.w/.l and nm.b/.w/.l set the width; bare is a
                  word. Writes into the monitor are refused.
  mtest <start> <end> [pattern [iters]] DESTRUCTIVE RAM test
                  writes and reads back every word in start..end, so
                  the range is OVERWRITTEN and NOT restored. No default
                  range and it must lie inside a payload window - it
                  refuses the monitor and everything else you do not
                  own. Address, moving-inversion and walking one/zero
                  tests; iters defaults to 1 (it does not loop forever)
                  and any key stops it. A true DRAM test only with the
                  D-cache off, which is the boot default.
  base [address]
                  a default address added to the address arguments of
                  memory, write, fill, copy and compare, so repeated
                  calls stop needing one. Starts at zero. It is NOT
                  added by crc32 - which matches U-Boot - nor by
                  readback, which is in the same family, and every
                  command that does add it says so on the line.
                  base 0 turns it off.
  force <address>                       override one refused address
                  EVERY command above that takes an address from you
                  asks the board first whether that address is safe to
                  touch, and refuses if it is not. This is what lets
                  you go ahead anyway.
                  Why it exists: on one of the boards Anvil runs on, a
                  read of a block whose clock is off does not fail -
                  the processor stops on it and the board has to be
                  unplugged. A single memory command has done that
                  three times. The board keeps a list of the blocks it
                  knows about, and a refusal names the block and says
                  whether the answer is measured or merely unknown.
                  How it works: type force and the address, then
                  repeat the refused command on the very NEXT line.
                  It arms exactly that one address, for exactly one
                  command line, and then expires whether it was used
                  or not. force on its own says what is armed; force
                  off disarms early.
                  Why two lines and not a flag on the command: a flag
                  is something a script can carry without anybody
                  having decided, and deciding is the entire point.
                  Writing the address twice, under two command words,
                  cannot happen by accident.
                  Type info to see what this board knows and where
                  each answer came from.
  Coming from U-Boot: md is memory, mw is fill, cmp is compare and cp
  is copy, and all four of those U-Boot spellings are accepted here, so
  a line copied out of a U-Boot session still runs. mm, nm and mtest
  keep their U-Boot names.
  <the .b/.w/.l width rule, worked out from the width table at run time>
  loop is deliberately absent - it cannot return at all.
  info                                  [i, board]
  uptime                                [up]
                  what board this is, how hot it is, and every clock
                  rate the firmware will tell us about.
  messages        what background services reported - a lease, the
                  radio rekeying or recovering, the network console
                  arming on a new address. They are never printed on
                  the command line; this is where they are read, and
                  a screen shows the newest one on the banner until
                  this has been run.
  clock [rate]                          [c]
                  show or set the processor clock. The rate is in
                  hertz and it is DECIMAL - the one decimal argument
                  in this monitor. It prints what the firmware
                  applied and then what is actually measured,
                  separately, because the firmware clamps a rate it
                  dislikes and still reports success.
  time [status]
                  live wall time, zone, provenance and synchronization
                  state. An unset clock says so; a restored disk value
                  is identified as a floor, not trusted current time.
  time set <unix-seconds-UTC>
                  set trusted manual UTC time from decimal Unix seconds.
  time zone <UTC | America/Chicago | fixed:+HH:MM | fixed:-HH:MM>
                  choose display civil time. America/Chicago applies
                  CST/CDT automatically; a fixed offset never does.
(only on a board with NET:)
  time sync       schedule a nonblocking SNTP refresh now.
  time server <IPv4-or-hostname | default>
                  choose SNTP explicitly, or restore DHCP option 42 then
                  time.cloudflare.com fallback. A server never chooses
                  the zone. Plain SNTP is not authenticated.
                  Unknown zones/servers are refused. Time changes stay
                  in memory until settings save. Default display is UTC.

FROM U-BOOT, AND HARDWARE-FREE
  echo [-n] <args>
                  print the arguments, separated by single spaces, then
                  a newline. -n as the first word drops the newline. No
                  variable expansion - this monitor has no shell, so
                  echo $x prints those three characters.
  sleep <seconds>
                  wait that many seconds and come back. Decimal seconds
                  - a leading 0x or $ is hex, like clock. Any key ends
                  the wait early, because a wait that could not be
                  broken would be a hang. The ceiling is a day.
  version [full]                        [ver]
                  what this monitor is, WHICH build it is, and which
                  target it was built for. The board name, the
                  processor, the exception level and the target all
                  come from the board, so this describes THIS computer
                  and not some other one.
                  It prints the build number with its date and time,
                  and this image's own size and extent - those two
                  together already tell two builds apart.
                  version full adds a crc32 over the running image:
                  the digest that says WHAT is in it rather than which
                  build it is. It is a separate word because it reads
                  every byte and is not instant, and bare version
                  prints the exact crc32 command instead.
                  Unlike U-Boot it does not print a compiler or
                  linker version, because neither is stamped into the
                  image and a guessed one is worse than none.
  setexpr <name> <val1> [<op> <val2>]
                  work out an expression and store it in the settings
                  store as hex. op is one of + - * / % & | ^ << >>, both
                  values hex. setexpr addr 400000 + 1000 puts 401000 in
                  the setting called addr, ready for memory or run to use.
                  The *addr, fmt and gsub forms are not here yet.

THE SCREEN
  screen [on [dsi | hdmi | number] | off | displays
          | rotate [0|90|180|270]]              [s]
                  the console on a screen. Everything the serial
                  line gets, the screen gets; the wire stays the
                  complete record and the screen is the
                  convenience.
                  THERE ARE TWO KINDS OF SCREEN ON THIS BOARD and
                  they are not the same thing. An HDMI display is
                  the firmware's: it must be connected BEFORE the
                  board powers on, because the firmware only looks
                  at boot. The Waveshare DSI panel is THIS
                  monitor's - the firmware owns no DSI display and
                  never brings DSI1 up, so this monitor lights the
                  panel itself out of its own memory.
                  AT BOOT, WITH NOTHING TYPED: a DSI panel that
                  answers on the display connector wins, because
                  somebody physically plugged it in; otherwise an
                  HDMI display if the firmware found one;
                  otherwise no screen, which is not a failure. The
                  boot log says which.
                  screen on its own says whether it is on, and
                  turns it on if it is off. screen on dsi and
                  screen on hdmi move it between the two.
                  screen displays lists BOTH kinds truthfully -
                  the firmware's census and the panel separately,
                  because the panel is not one of the firmware's
                  displays and reporting it as one would be an
                  invention. This board has two HDMI sockets;
                  screen on 1 brings the console up on the second
                  display in that list. The number is a position
                  in the list, NOT the number on the socket: with
                  one cable, in either socket, it is number 0.
                  Plain screen on lets the firmware choose among
                  its own, which is what it has always done.
  screen rotate [0|90|180|270]
                  which way up the console sits ON THE DSI PANEL.
                  The panel SCANS 800 across by 1280 down and no
                  setting changes that, but it is mounted long
                  edge across, so THE DEFAULT IS 90 - landscape,
                  1280 by 800, 160 columns by 42 lines. IF THE
                  PICTURE IS UPSIDE DOWN, type
                  screen rotate 270 once: which of the two is the
                  top depends on how the flat cable leaves the
                  board, the setting is SAVED, and the panel comes
                  up that way afterwards with nothing typed.
                  Nobody rebuilds the monitor to turn a screen.
                  THE COST, said every time you ask: this hardware
                  has no 90 degree rotation - the video scaler can
                  mirror but not turn - so 90 and 270 draw into a
                  buffer of their own and transpose every repaint
                  onto the panel, and a scroll becomes a full
                  repaint. 0 and 180 move no pixel and keep the
                  hardware scroll, and 0 is 100 columns by 72
                  lines of THE SAME SIZE type, standing on its
                  side - taller and narrower, not smaller. The
                  letters are the same physical size at every
                  rotation; see screen scale for why.
                  Rotation is the panel's: HDMI is landscape as
                  the firmware hands it over and is not turned.
  screen scale [n|auto]
                  how big the type is. IT IS NORMALLY COMPUTED:
                  this monitor works out how many pixels there
                  are to the inch on whatever screen it is
                  drawing on - the diagonal in pixels over the
                  diagonal in inches - and magnifies its 8 by 16
                  font by the whole number nearest 0.110 inch to
                  a line, which is what reads at a bench. Both of
                  those are facts about the GLASS and neither
                  changes when the picture is turned, which is
                  why turning the console no longer changes the
                  size of a letter. The DSI panel reports its own
                  size over I2C - 10.1 inches, 149 pixels to the
                  inch, magnification 1. NOTHING ON AN HDMI
                  DISPLAY CAN SAY HOW BIG IT IS, so 24 inches is
                  assumed and every report that uses it says so.
                  screen scale <n> overrides all of that if it
                  does not suit your eyes or your distance from
                  the screen, and it is SAVED; screen scale auto
                  forgets it and goes back to the calculation.
                  The boot log and screen print the density, the
                  magnification, the columns and rows, and the
                  height of a line in inches.
(only on a board with TOUCH:)
  screen keyboard [show|hide|state]
                  put the touch keyboard on the panel, take it
                  away, or describe it - from ANY console channel,
                  including this one. It goes through the same
                  path a finger on the prompt line takes, so what
                  it opens is the keyboard, not a picture of one:
                  the console gives up its bottom rows without
                  losing a character of what is on them, and the
                  keys type into the same line this wire does.
                  The key labels are set in the anti-aliased face
                  the banner's title uses, on both renderers.
  screenshot                            [p]
                  send a picture of the screen back over this wire.
                  It is run-length encoded, because the raw picture
                  would take twenty minutes at 115200 baud, and
                  tools/pmfshot.py on the host turns it into a PNG.
                  It takes several minutes. Only Ctrl-C stops it, so
                  that a stray keypress cannot throw the capture
                  away, and a stopped one is marked as stopped so
                  the host never writes half a picture.
  shot
                  send the KEPT picture - the frame a payload left
                  on the screen, copied out of the way before this
                  monitor repainted over it. Same format as
                  screenshot, so the same host tool decodes it, with
                  one machine line of header in front of it.
  shot arm
                  keep the frame the NEXT payload leaves behind,
                  whether or not it asks. Armed for one run.
  shot now        keep the screen as it is at this instant
  shot status     whether a capture is armed, and what is kept

OVER THE NETWORK
  This board has a gigabit Ethernet socket and this is what it is for:
  a 260 KB image takes twenty-four seconds down the serial line and well
  under a second over the wire. It speaks TFTP, which is what every
  board has been fetched over since 1981 and what U-Boot uses, so any
  machine that can serve a file to a router can serve one to this.
  get <name> [address]
                  fetch a file from the TFTP server into memory. The
                  name is the file as the server knows it; the address
                  is hex and defaults to <address>, the same place load
                  uses. The destination must be inside a payload window,
                  and the transfer stops at that window's end rather
                  than writing past it - a TFTP client does not know how
                  long a file is until it ends, so the room is checked
                  instead of the length.
  put <name> <address> <length>
                  send that many bytes of memory to the server as a
                  file. Both numbers hex, the length in bytes. Most
                  servers refuse to be written to until they are told to
                  allow it, and the server's own refusal is printed here
                  word for word when that happens.
  net             the four addresses and the state of the wire. This is
                  the command to type when get or put has failed,
                  because it names the step that is missing.
                  ONLY net server IS NEEDED FOR A TRANSFER. The other
                  three are the SAVED-ADDRESS source, one of the three
                  ways an interface can come to hold an address; get
                  and put read this board's own address, netmask and
                  gateway off whichever interface can reach the
                  server, whether that address came from a lease, from
                  these settings, or from the board probing one for
                  itself on a bare cable.
  net address <a.b.c.d>      the address this board answers to
  net netmask <a.b.c.d>      also spelled net mask
  net gateway <a.b.c.d>      also spelled net router. Use 0.0.0.0 when
                             there is no router, which is the truth on a
                             cable straight between two machines.
  net server <a.b.c.d>       the machine serving the files
  net dns <a.b.c.d>          the DNS resolver, for dns and ping by name
  net up          bring the Ethernet up now and report every step. get
                  and put do it themselves; this is the diagnostic.
  net down        stop it. It is also stopped automatically before every
                  run, because a payload must not share memory with a
                  controller that is still writing into it.
  net forget      take all four addresses back out
  net stats       WHAT THE NETWORK CONTROLLER ITSELF COUNTED on the
                  interface now in use - pause frames sent and received,
                  framing errors, dropped frames, and how many times the
                  link has been brought up or seen to drop. A counter
                  that reads zero is not printed, so anything you see is
                  a number worth reading. This is the command to type
                  when the MACHINE AT THE OTHER END of a cable is
                  misbehaving: net says what this monitor did, net stats
                  says what the hardware saw. Also spelled net counters.
  http serve [port]  start public HTTP pages (default port 8080)
  http status        show the server; http stop closes it
                     Plain HTTP, / and /health only; no accounts.
                     Cooperative prompt service with bounded client slots.
  net recv <port> <addr> [max-length]
                  RECEIVE ONE IMAGE OVER A TCP CONNECTION, into memory
                  at that address, and print how many bytes arrived and
                  the SHA-256 of what is now in that memory. This is the
                  fast way in: the same image over the serial line at
                  115200 is about two minutes. The port is decimal and
                  the address is hexadecimal; leave the length out and
                  the rest of that payload window is the ceiling.
                  The listener is opened for ONE connection and closed
                  again whatever happens, nothing is booted, and nothing
                  is written to the medium - boot mem <addr> enters a
                  container and save <name> <addr> <len> writes a file.
                  A peer that sends more than the window holds is cut
                  off AT the last allowed byte, never past it.
  ping <host>     send ICMP echo requests and time the replies, one a
                  second, until a key is pressed. The host is a dotted-
                  quad, or a name if a DNS server is set. It prints each
                  reply's measured round trip and a loss/min/avg/max
                  summary at the end.
  dns <hostname>  look a name up and print the address(es). Needs a DNS
                  server - net dns, or dhcp. Refuses honestly with none.
  dhcp            acquire an address by DHCP and report the IP, netmask,
                  gateway, DNS server and lease. On success it sets the
                  interface's runtime lease, so ping and dns work at once.
                  DHCP option 42 is retained per lease for the
                  nonblocking SNTP clock service when a server supplies it.
                  It does not overwrite saved static addresses or set a
                  TFTP server, so get and put still need net server -
                  and that one address is all they need.
  The four addresses live in the settings store, under net.address,
  net.netmask, net.gateway and net.server, so settings save keeps them
  and settings load brings them back. Coming from U-Boot, those four are
  its ipaddr, netmask, gatewayip and serverip.
  tftpboot and tftpput are NOT accepted as aliases, deliberately.
  U-Boot takes the address first and the name second and this monitor
  takes the name first, to match its own load and save. An alias whose
  arguments mean something else is worse than no alias: a line pasted
  out of a U-Boot session would run, and fetch a file called 0x400000.

SETTINGS THAT SURVIVE A POWER CYCLE
  This is what U-Boot's printenv, setenv and saveenv were for, and those
  three names now work here too, over this same store:
    printenv [name...]         settings show, or the named settings
    setenv <name> <value>      settings set. With no value it does NOT
                               delete (U-Boot does) - use settings
                               remove, so a keystroke cannot quietly
                               destroy a setting.
    saveenv                    settings save
    env print / set / save / load / delete <name>
                               the same, spelled U-Boot's env <sub> way
    env exists <name>          say whether one is set
    env grep <text>            list the ones whose name or value has it

  THE PERSISTED BOOT TARGET lives in this same store, as four names:
    boot.file       the container to boot at start-up, e.g. APP.PMF.
                    Unset, this board goes straight to its prompt and
                    runs nothing by itself - and waits for nothing,
                    because a countdown that can only end one way
                    teaches people to ignore countdowns.
    boot.delay      seconds to count down first. Default 2. Any key
                    during it drops to this prompt, and the failure
                    counter is not touched - nothing was attempted.
    boot.fails      attempts since anything last confirmed a good
                    boot. THE REBOOT-LOOP GUARD. It is written to the
                    medium BEFORE each attempt, not after, because a
                    payload that hangs never gets to an after.
    boot.maxfails   how many attempts before this monitor stops
                    trying and says why. Default 3.
  A payload marks itself good by getting boot.fails back to 0. The
  operator types boot ok; a payload that RETURNS can have the operator
  do it; a payload that keeps the board writes the setting through this
  same store before it takes over - set boot.fails to 0 and save. The
  guard exists because a bootloader that enters a payload automatically
  has invented a way to lose a board: a payload that hangs is re-entered
  every start, and there is then never a prompt long enough to fix it.
    setenv boot.file APP.PMF
    saveenv
  is the whole of arming it.
  A password is still masked by printenv, the same as settings show,
  because this output reaches the HDMI console and the next screenshot;
  settings reveal prints one in full. Up to
  thirty-two names and values, kept in memory and written to a plain
  text file called SETTINGS.TXT in the root of the boot medium. That
  file opens in any text editor on any computer, which is the recovery
  story: a board that will not boot because of something in its
  settings is fixed by pulling the stick and deleting a line.
  settings                              [settings show]
                  list everything. Anything whose name contains
                  password, passphrase or secret is HIDDEN, because
                  this output also goes to the HDMI console and into
                  the next screenshot. The true length is shown.
  settings set <name> <value>
                  the value is the whole rest of the line, so it may
                  contain spaces. The input line is 144 characters,
                  which is the longest legal one of these - a
                  31-character name and a 95-character value - so
                  nothing has to be set by editing the file any more.
  settings remove <name>
  settings reveal <name>
                  print one in full, hidden or not. The deliberate
                  keystroke that puts a password on the screen.
  settings save   write SETTINGS.TXT through this board's file writer;
                  availability depends on the mounted medium. The
                  whole file is rewritten, so hand-typed comments in it
                  are lost.
  settings load   read it back. Nothing loads it for you: bringing the
                  medium up is slow and noisy and the prompt comes
                  first.
  settings discard
                  a load that hit a bad line stops there and blocks the
                  next save, because saving would delete the lines it
                  never read. This says throw them away.
  wifi            list every network slot, passphrases hidden. wifi
                  show is the same command spelled out. FOUR networks
                  can be stored and THE SLOT NUMBER IS THE ORDER THEY
                  WOULD BE TRIED IN - slot 1 first. Put the one you
                  most want joined in slot 1.
  wifi ssid <slot> <name>
                  the name is the rest of the line, so it may contain
                  spaces. One to thirty-two characters.
  wifi phrase <slot> <phrase>
                  the passphrase for that slot, the rest of the line,
                  8 to 63 characters, and STORED IN PLAIN TEXT - the
                  command says so at length every time. Give this
                  board a guest network. It is a DIFFERENT WORD from
                  wifi password because that one takes the whole rest
                  of the line, so a slot number in front of it could
                  not be told from the start of a passphrase.
  wifi find <name>
                  which slot holds that name. The comparison is EXACT:
                  case counts and a 2.4ghz suffix is part of the name,
                  because two real networks here differ by no more.
  wifi forget <slot>
                  clear one slot, name and passphrase together. The
                  others do not move up - the numbers are a preference
                  order and renumbering them would change it.
  wifi keys       the settings names the slots live under, to hand to
                  settings reveal.
  The single network this monitor used to keep is still there and is
  still READ - LAST, after every numbered slot - so a stick written by
  an older build keeps working and no saved passphrase went missing:
  wifi network <name>       the name is the rest of the line
  wifi password <phrase>    also spelled wifi passphrase
  wifi forget     take that pair back out. It does NOT touch the slots.
  wifi incidents  every Wi-Fi failure on record (WIFILOG.TXT on the stick):
                  what the radio saw before it, saved before recovery,
                  and each recovery step and how it ended.
  wifi rekey ask [group|pair]  ask the access point to rekey right now.
  wifi deaf <s> [ask]  leave the radio unserviced for s seconds, the way a
                  payload does; with ask the access point is asked to rekey
                  first, so it kicks the board while nobody listens.
  wifi iovar <name>  read one 32-bit firmware variable as the radio holds
                  it now (bcn_timeout, roam_off, assoc_listen ...).
  wifi scan       bring the radio up and list the stored networks that
                  are on the air now (needs BRCMFW.BIN, BRCMNV.TXT and
                  BRCMCLM.BLB on the stick).

THE BOARD
  gpio [status] [all | <pin>]
                  report the general-purpose I/O pins: each pin's
                  function, its level read back from the actual pad, and
                  its pull. With no argument it shows the user-header
                  pins; gpio all shows every line the board has; gpio
                  with a pin number shows one. status is the default and
                  may be written out (gpio status, gpio status all, gpio
                  status 21). Reading any pin is always allowed.
  gpio set <pin>
  gpio clear <pin>
                  drive a pin high or low. This makes the pin an output,
                  and says so. The line printed back is the ACTUAL pad
                  read after the write, not what was asked for.
  gpio toggle <pin>
                  invert an output pin. A pin that is not already an
                  output has nothing to invert and is refused - use set
                  or clear to start driving one.
  gpio output <pin>
  gpio input <pin>
                  set the pin's direction, without driving a level.
                  PINS ARE DECIMAL, like clock and unlike the memory
                  commands - a GPIO number is written in decimal on the
                  header and in the datasheet. A leading 0x or $ still
                  forces hex.
                  A WRITE to a pin the board itself is using is refused
                  with a sentence naming the function, not a silent no-op:
                  on this board that is the serial console (GPIO 14/15)
                  and the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth radio's bus (GPIO 34-39). The
                  micro-SD card is on a dedicated socket, not a GPIO, so
                  it needs no such guard.
                  A board with no GPIO says so and does nothing, because
                  Anvil is one monitor across many boards and not every
                  board has pins to report.
  fan [status]
  fan pin <gpio> | none
  fan auto | off | on | <percent>
  fan curve <lowF> <highF>
  fan hyst <degreesF>
  fan hz <n>
                  the fan, the part's own temperature, and the curve
                  between them. EVERY TEMPERATURE HERE IS FAHRENHEIT,
                  typed and printed. fan on its own prints the reading in
                  whole degrees F, with the celsius and the raw
                  millidegrees in brackets so the number can be checked
                  against a datasheet or another tool; which of the
                  board's two thermometers answered; the mode, the duty,
                  the pin, and the pins the board will drive - a star
                  marks the
                  ones with a real modulator behind them, which are
                  steady at any frequency and are what a four-wire fan
                  wants; the rest are toggled by software from this
                  prompt's own idle loop, which is fine for a two-wire
                  fan on a transistor and is COARSE - it stops
                  modulating while a long command runs and parks the pin
                  at the level the board considers safe.
                  NO PIN IS DRIVEN UNTIL ONE IS NAMED. The board does
                  not know where a fan is wired, so fan pin <gpio> is
                  the first thing to type and it is remembered.
                  auto lets the curve decide: off below the low
                  temperature, ramping to full at the high one, with a
                  few degrees of hysteresis so it does not hunt, a brief
                  full-speed kick to get a stationary fan turning, and
                  FULL SPEED whenever no temperature can be read at all.
                  It starts at off below 113 F, full at 158 F, with 5 F
                  of hysteresis - which is where this part idles quiet
                  and where it still has headroom before the firmware
                  starts slowing it down at 185 F.
                  off and on override it; a bare percentage holds a duty.
                  Degrees, percentages, pins and hertz are all DECIMAL.
                  A CURVE SAVED BY A BUILD FROM BEFORE 2026-09-07 IS IN
                  CELSIUS. It is converted on the way in and the boot log
                  says so; type settings save to write the converted
                  numbers back.
                  Settings are remembered in the table but NOT written to
                  the file until settings save, like every other setting.
                  A board with no modulator, or no thermometer, says so
                  and does nothing.
  i2c probe
  i2c read  <addr> <reg> [count]
  i2c write <addr> <reg> <byte...>
  i2c speed [hz]
                  talk to devices on the header I2C bus (SDA/SCL on
                  GPIO 2 and 3). probe lists every 7-bit address that
                  answers; read points a device at a register and reads
                  count bytes (default 1); write sends a register then
                  one or more data bytes. Addresses, registers, bytes
                  and count are HEX; the speed is DECIMAL, like clock.
                  A register read puts a STOP between the pointer write
                  and the read, not a repeated start, so a device that
                  needs a repeated start will not read right. On a NACK
                  or a wedged bus it says which one happened and that it
                  did nothing. A board with no I2C says so and does
                  nothing. The clock rate shown is derived from the
                  divider source MEASURED on the pin, not the nominal.
(only on a board with TOUCH:)
  touch [points | panel power|prepare|light <n>|reset |
         bus display|header | axes <s> <x> <y>]
                  the DSI panel's touch controller and its power MCU.
                  NOT the bus above: this one is BSC0 on GPIO 44 and 45
                  at ALT1, the display and camera connectors, and it is
                  the default here because that is where the panel is
                  plugged in. No jumper wires. It puts the header bus
                  back when it finishes so i2c never names the wrong
                  pair of wires. touch on its own says what answered and
                  what it is, and prints the pads before and after the
                  mux - both lines low on THIS bus is a cable answer,
                  because its pull-ups are on the panel board. panel
                  power is the MCU's own probe write; panel prepare is
                  the panel's rails and reset; panel light takes a
                  DECIMAL 0 to 255 and is NOT inverted on this
                  generation; panel reset pulses the touch chip's reset,
                  which is a pin on that MCU and on no Pi GPIO - so the
                  touch chip cannot answer until panel power has run.
                  points reports live coordinates until a key is pressed -
                  raw, and where each one lands on the console.
                  THERE IS NOTHING TO TURN ON. A finger moves the SAME
                  cursor a USB mouse moves and a tap presses the same
                  button, with nothing typed, whenever the console is on
                  the panel. Where a contact lands is worked out by the
                  DISPLAY layer, through the same rotation and scale the
                  picture uses, so screen rotate turns the finger with the
                  console and needs nothing typed here. axes on its own
                  shows the mapping in force, and where the corners land
                  once the controller has said how big it is. With three
                  0-or-1 numbers it sets the one correction an eye may
                  still have to make - which way the touch chip counts
                  against the panel it is glued to - and it is SAVED, so
                  it is typed once.
  mod [list | info <file> | devices | seams | load <file> [seam] |
       unload <file> | detach <seam>]
                  driver modules. Not every board has the same hardware,
                  so a driver can live in a .MOD file on the card instead
                  of inside this monitor. MODULES.TXT in the root, one
                  file name per line, loads them at boot - each is
                  verified against its own digest, placed in a reserved
                  arena, matched to a device this board declares, probed
                  without side effects and initialised exactly once. mod
                  on its own lists what is loaded, where and in what
                  state; devices lists what is here to drive and seams
                  lists what each service is answered by. An optional
                  seam name NARROWS a module to part of what its header
                  declares and can never widen it. unload is REFUSED while
                  anything is still using the service - detach asks those
                  users to let go first, and they fall back to whatever
                  they used before the module was loaded. An unloaded
                  module's memory stays reserved until a reset.
  mmc [info | read <blk> <addr> [count] | write <blk> <addr> [count]]
                  raw block access to the SD card, with no filesystem -
                  this is the card underneath mount/load, seen as 512-byte
                  blocks. mmc on its own, or mmc info, prints the card's
                  class, block size, block count and capacity. mmc read
                  copies count blocks (default 1) from the card at block
                  <blk> into RAM at <addr>; mmc write copies them the other
                  way, from RAM onto the card. ALL THREE NUMBERS ARE HEX -
                  <blk> a block index, <addr> a RAM byte address, <count> a
                  number of blocks. The RAM address must be 4-byte aligned
                  and a range that touches the monitor is refused, both for
                  read and for write. mmc write is destructive and
                  unconditional: it overwrites raw blocks, a filesystem
                  included, with no undo and no are-you-sure. A board with
                  no card controller says so and does nothing; a board that
                  can read but not write refuses mmc write and says why.
  usb [info | tree | link | storage | read <blk> <addr> [count]]
  gnss [watch [s] | raw [s] | source usb|bluetooth|ble|network]   a satellite receiver
  https get <url>   fetch a page over TLS 1.3, verified against the root store
  tls [roots|reload]   the TLS connection and the root store (2:/tls/roots.pem)
                  look at the USB bus. usb, or usb info, lists the host
                  controller, the ports and every device that answered
                  enumeration - its speed, its VID:PID and its class. usb
                  tree draws the topology: controller, root ports, the
                  internal hub and its ports. usb link prints the raw
                  registers of the link the controller sits on - the
                  clock, the trained speed and width, the inbound window
                  and the power policy - which is the evidence behind the
                  one sentence usb tree summarises them in. usb storage
                  reports a
                  memory stick's vendor, block size and capacity. usb
                  read pulls raw 512-byte blocks off the stick straight
                  into memory, without a filesystem: the block number,
                  the destination and the count are ALL hexadecimal, and
                  the destination is range-checked against the payload
                  windows exactly like load. It shows what the stack
                  already drives for mount and the cursor; it starts and
                  resets nothing. A board with no USB host says so and
                  does nothing.
  font info
                  list the four resident TrueType slots, selected face,
                  file sizes and basic metrics. font load <slot> <path>
                  reads a static TrueType file of at most 1024 KiB into
                  an empty slot only after structural validation; failed
                  loads preserve the current selection. font select <slot>
                  binds a loaded face; `font select bitmap` returns to the
                  built-in face. font unload <slot> frees a slot and
                  returns to the built-in bitmap face if it was selected.
  baud [rate]
                  change how fast this serial line runs. The clock
                  feeding the serial port on this board is 48 MHz,
                  so 1500000 and 3000000 divide into it exactly -
                  thirteen and twenty-six times the default. Reopen
                  the port at the new rate and press Enter. If
                  nothing answers within eight seconds the board
                  puts 115200 back by itself, so a rate your adapter
                  cannot manage costs a pause and not a power cycle.
  reset                                 [r, reboot]
                  reset the board immediately. The firmware reloads
                  this monitor from the stick. There is no are-you-sure
                  question, on purpose: the cost of being wrong is
                  a five second reboot into a working loader.
  help                                  [h, ?, commands]
                  print this. A question mark on its own does the
                  same thing.

WHERE A PAYLOAD MAY GO
These are the two windows of memory a payload may be loaded into:
  <this board's payload windows, printed at run time>
  The gap between them holds this monitor, the three parked processor
  cores, and a stretch where there is no DRAM at all. A payload may not
  straddle that gap, and one that tries is refused rather than half
  written.
WHAT THIS MONITOR OWNS
  <this board's memory map, printed at run time>
  Every command that writes memory refuses to write into any of it,
  and the refusal names the region.
  Load a payload at the staging address on that line, whatever it was
  built for: an image is the same bytes at any --load-addr, so one
  made last month wants staging here rather than rebuilding. Leave
  512 KiB above the base clear - that is where its own uninitialised
  data goes, and nothing here checks it for you.
  The other window starts at 0x<address>.
  Add --entry-returns if you want the payload to come back to this
  prompt and have its x0 register printed. A stock image never comes
  back at all.
@ENDFRAG

@SECTION Raspberry Pi 4 adds

@FRAG

PROGRAMS
  programs             the payload containers (.pmf) on the boot medium
  <name>               a listed name typed on its own runs that program

PI 4 EL3 ACCEPTANCE
  el3test              one bounded secure-timer IRQ, then one controlled BRK
  coretest status      resident secondary-core ownership and last result
  coretest run         16 coherent job rounds on cores 1, 2 and 3
  coretest stop        acknowledge and permanently park those workers
These are explicit diagnostics, never boot actions. After coretest run,
restart before changing cache policy or entering a payload.
@ENDFRAG
